0.value:
mgl_camera and mgl_orbit_camera decide where the scene is seen from.

THE NODES:

mgl_camera        a fixed viewpoint: a position, a target and a field of view
mgl_orbit_camera  a viewpoint you can drag - it takes the context's interaction
                  events and turns them into yaw, elevation and distance

They are two forms of the same thing. Both set the view and the projection for whatever is drawn after them; they differ only in how you say where the eye is.

YOU DO NOT NEED ONE TO SEE SOMETHING:
mgl_context supplies a default camera (at 0 0 3, looking at the origin), switchable with its 'default_camera' option and adjustable with its 'camera_' options. A camera node replaces that view for everything drawn after it.

A CAMERA IS NOT PUT BACK:
Transforms, colours and materials are undone at the end of the branch they sit in. A camera is not: it sets the view for the rest of the frame, including branches drawn after its own. So it belongs near the top of the chain, before anything it should see. Two cameras in one chain means the second one wins for everything after it.

THE ORBIT CAMERA:
The eye sits on a sphere around 'target'. 'distance' is the radius, 'yaw' the angle around the vertical in degrees - 0 puts the eye on the plus z side - and 'elevation' the angle above the horizontal.

Patch the context's 'ui' outlet into its 'ui' inlet and the picture becomes the control: dragging with the left button orbits (elevation stops at 89 degrees either way), and the scroll wheel zooms by changing the distance. The events come from the context's own picture - its window or fullscreen view, or the picture inside the node when the context's 'node_mouse_events' option is ticked, as here.

The messages top, bottom, front, back, left and right snap it to that view, keeping target and distance. 'front' looks at a subject facing minus z from in front of it; 'side' is an older name for 'right'.

ORTHOGRAPHIC:
The orbit camera's 'projection' option can be orthographic - no perspective, parallel lines stay parallel. The picture keeps the same scale at the target when you switch, and zooming still works, because the visible height is set from distance and field of view. In that mode 'near' is not used, and 'far' is the half-depth of the slab drawn, centred on the target.

SYNTAX:
mgl_camera
mgl_orbit_camera

EXAMPLE:
mgl_orbit_camera

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

mgl chain in:
The chain. This is what triggers the node.

fov (both):
The vertical field of view in degrees, 60 by default. Wide values exaggerate depth; narrow ones flatten it.

pos / target / up (mgl_camera):
Where the camera is (0 0 3), what it looks at (the origin), and which way is up (0 1 0).

target / distance / yaw / elevation (mgl_orbit_camera):
What to orbit around, how far away (3), and where on the orbit (yaw 0, elevation 20).

ui (mgl_orbit_camera):
Interaction events from mgl_context's 'ui' outlet.

near / far (options, both):
The nearest and farthest distances drawn, 0.1 and 100.

projection / drag_speed / zoom_speed (options, mgl_orbit_camera):
Perspective or orthographic, and how fast dragging and scrolling move it.

OUTPUTS:

mgl chain out:
The chain, seen from this camera.

RELATED:
mgl_context for the default camera. mgl_light, mgl_material and mgl_color used to share this page.
